- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model shows gradual upward drift, cap the forecast rise to avoid overshoot after recent spikes.
- If supply net is strongly negative (e.g., -20+), model must adjust downward faster than historical mean reversion; don’t assume momentum continues.
- After a sharp spike (e.g., >75), model should not continue rising for 3+ days — expect mean reversion or volatility decay.
- When bullish sentiment is high but supply net is negative, model should not ignore event-driven supply shocks — adjust downward if auction supply is high.
- If sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and price is trending upward, model should not over-forecast — reduce slope to avoid lagged reaction.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from 15-day moving average, model must re-estimate baseline using sentiment-weighted recent history.
- When bullish sentiment is low (≤0.33) and supply net is negative, model should not assume price will rise — expect downward correction or volatility pause.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome spikes, model must re-estimate horizon-specific bias — especially if sentiment is bullish but supply is high.
- For auctions with high supply net, model must reduce forecast by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or bearish — avoid overconfidence in auction-driven price moves.
- If sentiment is bullish but true outcome is flat or falling, model must re-estimate horizon — consider event-driven supply shocks or policy changes.
